opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people often underestimate how much of what scientists do is shaped by norms rather than by incentives alone. The standard story is that if you don't do the research, someone else will, so your individual restraint makes no difference. But that story assumes the pool of people capable of doing cutting-edge work is enormous and interchangeable, and at the frontier it really isn't. There are a relatively small number of people with the skills to push certain capabilities forward, and if a meaningful fraction of them come to see certain kinds of work as genuinely wrong, the way many physicists came to see weapons work, or the way biologists came to view certain recombinant DNA experiments in the 1970s, that actually slows things down.

There's also a historical pattern worth noticing. Asilomar is an interesting example: researchers themselves paused and set guidelines before governments had really caught up. That didn't happen because the competitive pressures vanished. It happened because the community developed a shared sense that some lines shouldn't be crossed lightly, and that shared sense made it costly, reputationally and socially, to be the person who defected.

And moral attitudes feed into everything else. Companies need to recruit these people. If top researchers won't work on something, or will leave and speak publicly if asked to, that changes what labs are willing to attempt. It also changes what governments think is politically feasible, because regulation is much easier when the experts themselves are asking for it rather than fighting it.

So I don't think norms are a complete solution. Competitive pressures are real, and you need institutions and eventually international agreements. But changing how researchers see their own responsibility is one of the cheaper and faster levers we have, and it makes all the other levers work better.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers may come to view certain work as wrong, making them less willing to pursue it; refusal, departure, and reputational costs can slow research despite competitive pressures.

r002.rationale: The response does not contrast expectations about widespread human genetic enhancement with its later lack of widespread adoption.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss human cloning or genetic enhancement as evidence about restraint without intensive international laboratory verification.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: I think the competitive incentives are real, but people sometimes overstate how much they determine what actually happens. If you look at the history of other powerful technologies, moral attitudes among the researchers themselves have mattered quite a lot. Think about the biologists at Asilomar in the 1970s, who voluntarily paused certain recombinant DNA work until they had a better sense of the risks. Or the way that chemical and biological weapons became something that most scientists simply wouldn't work on, even when governments were willing to pay for it. Those norms didn't come from nowhere. They came from the scientific community deciding that some things were beneath them, and that doing them would cost you the respect of your peers.

And the thing about AI is that the number of people with the skills to do the frontier research is still fairly small. It's not like a commodity that anyone can produce. So if a substantial fraction of the best researchers come to see certain kinds of work as reckless or disreputable, that actually constrains what labs and governments can do, because they need those people. Talent is one of the key inputs, and talent has opinions.

I'd also say that competitive incentives aren't fixed features of the universe. They're partly shaped by what people believe is acceptable. If researchers care about safety, they push for it inside their organisations, they're more willing to support coordination between labs, they're more willing to blow the whistle, and they shape the culture that new people are trained into. Over time, that changes what the competition is even about. You can imagine a world where labs compete partly on being seen as responsible, rather than purely on capabilities, and that's much more likely if the people doing the work actually hold those values.

So I don't think changing attitudes is sufficient on its own. You still need institutions, regulation, international agreements and so on. But I'd see it as one of the foundations those other things rest on. It's very hard to get good governance of a technology when the people building it think the concerns are silly. And it's considerably easier when they share them.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers’ shared moral norms can make dangerous work seem reckless or disreputable, reducing willingness to pursue it and constraining labs’ access to talent despite competitive incentives.

r002.rationale: It gives examples involving recombinant DNA and weapons research, but does not contrast expectations of widespread genetic enhancement with its later lack of adoption.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss human cloning or genetic enhancement, or use their scarcity as evidence about international laboratory verification.

astra-6.text:
Well, competitive incentives matter, but they’re not the only things people respond to. Researchers also care about whether their work is good for the world, and about what their colleagues think of it. If they came to believe that a particular line of research was putting humanity at serious risk, that could give them a substantial reason not to pursue it.

You might worry that someone else would simply do the work instead. But that isn’t automatic: researchers aren’t perfectly interchangeable, and delaying a dangerous development could give us more time to make it safe. Moreover, if that moral concern became widespread within the research community, it could change professional norms and make collective restraint easier.

So I wouldn’t claim that changing attitudes is sufficient. We’d also want institutions that address the competitive pressures. But moral attitudes can help create those institutions, as well as influence what people do before they’re in place.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers’ moral concerns about serious risk can give them a substantial reason not to pursue dangerous research, countering competitive incentives.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about earlier expectations of widespread genetic enhancement or its subsequent adoption.

r003.rationale: It mentions neither cloning nor genetic enhancement, and makes no claim about international laboratory verification.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, competitive incentives are powerful, but they’re not the only thing motivating researchers. People also care about whether their work is good for the world, and about what their colleagues think of it. If you come to believe that a particular line of research poses an unacceptable risk, that can give you a reason not to pursue it, even if doing so would advance your career.

Of course, there’s the objection that if you don’t do it, someone else will. But that isn’t always true, especially when the relevant expertise is scarce. And even when someone else eventually would, delaying the work could give us valuable time to develop safeguards.

The larger effect would come from changing shared norms. If enough researchers regard certain work as irresponsible, that can change what people are willing to collaborate on and what institutions are willing to support. It doesn’t eliminate the need for coordination or regulation, but it can help make those things possible.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers’ concern for the good of the world and shared professional norms can give them reasons not to pursue risky work despite career incentives.

r002.rationale: The response does not contrast past expectations of widespread genetic enhancement with its later lack of widespread adoption.

r003.rationale: The response mentions scarce expertise in general, but does not cite cloning or genetic enhancement as evidence that restraint can work without intensive international laboratory verification.
